question:
**Clarify what we actually did.** Which modules did we implement and evaluate? What do route following and pedestrian-risk prediction do? Which elements come from existing methods, and which changes were developed for this project? Clearly distinguish completed work from the proposed but unimplemented local-detour extension.
**Use appropriate comparisons.** I questioned whether PPO was a suitable main baseline. Explain why we introduced Pure Pursuit, RPP-inspired and DWA-style controllers, together with distance-based yielding and the zero-velocity ablation. Explain what each comparison tests.
**Review the code and evaluation logic.** I requested closer inspection of the arrival criteria and failure cases, because a coarse success definition could misrepresent performance. Explain the corrections and checks already completed, using genuine three-dimensional simulator execution and recorded data.
**Interpret the results honestly.** The predictive method did not demonstrate an overall advantage. Explain the arrival outcomes and timing comparisons without attributing every difference to pedestrian-velocity prediction. Treat this as a small exploratory assignment rather than a SOTA claim. I**mprove the proposal’s argument and readability.** Connect the research question, urban spatial conditions, data, variables, spatial units, methods and practical implications. Use clear sections, explanatory transitions and full names for technical abbreviations. Move detailed software versions and engineering parameters outside the main text.**Keep the presentation appropriate for the assignment.** Retain a readable five-page main proposal, including figures and references. Use black headings and balanced spacing. Preserve previous proposal versions and experimental records.**Keep the AI-use record concise and accurate.** Focus on assistance with code changes, experimental comparisons, result checking and document revision.
response:
The completed work is a small, training-free MetaUrban pilot. It provides comparative evidence and failure analysis, but does not establish an overall advantage for predictive navigation.

1. **Implemented work.** Route following uses the reference route to select a point ahead, steer towards it and regulate speed around turns and the destination. Earlier corrections also addressed braking and stopping. The pedestrian-risk module evaluates candidate speeds, including stopping, over a 1.5-second horizon. It predicts motion along the route and compares robot and pedestrian body footprints. Pure Pursuit, regulated tracking, motion prediction and local command search are established ideas. This project implemented their local integration, risk-based speed selection, comparison variants and evaluation pipeline; it does not claim to have invented those ideas. The robot uses native three-dimensional simulator physics and privileged numerical states, not camera-based perception or humanoid locomotion.

2. **Comparison methods.** A pretrained Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) policy alone would mix policy-transfer limitations with changes to route information and control. The final classical suite therefore uses shared route/state inputs and does not execute that neural policy. Pure Pursuit (PP) with a static guard tests a simple tracker. Regulated Pure Pursuit (RPP)-inspired control tests reactive speed regulation. The Dynamic Window Approach (DWA)-style controller tests local speed and steering flexibility. These are local adaptations, not official reproductions. Distance-based yielding asks whether current distance is sufficient. The zero-velocity ablation keeps the forecast procedure but sets predicted pedestrian velocity to zero, isolating that input while actual pedestrians still move.

3. **Evaluation corrections and checks.** Strict arrival now requires both the native arrival flag and an endpoint distance of at most 2 m. Pre-step checks require route length and start-to-goal distance of at least 5 m. Contact-free arrival additionally excludes recorded pedestrian, object, building and sidewalk contacts. Failure and contact episodes remain in the analysis. Pedestrian contacts include both relevant native flags because pedestrian bodies can carry a vehicle tag. Existing acceptance checks compared initial scenes, replayed controller decisions and checked recorded geometry. A subsequent audit independently recomputed outcomes and metrics from 73,885 recorded decisions across 160 formal runs. Genuine simulator videos were checked against physics-only trajectories. These were automated checks with AI assistance, not new experiments in this revision.

4. **What the results show.** After 68 development runs, the completed tests comprised 120 main runs and 40 separately reported single-pedestrian diagnostic runs. In the main test, PP, RPP-inspired, distance-based yielding and both forecast versions each achieved 16/20 strict arrivals and 13/20 contact-free arrivals. DWA-style achieved 14/20 and 12/20. Forecasting was 3.16 seconds faster than RPP on their 16 jointly successful conditions, but 0.28 seconds slower than its zero-velocity ablation on those same conditions. The RPP comparison therefore does not demonstrate a benefit from measured pedestrian velocity or general efficiency superiority. Waiting time measures stop commands; proximity exposure is a geometric proxy, not human comfort.

5. **Proposed work and uncertainty.** The bounded-detour trigger remains unimplemented. It would consider limited left/right waypoint offsets after persistent stopping caused by static checks, preserve footprint buffers and remain within validated walkable space. Otherwise, the robot would keep waiting. The proposed 120-run comparison would test RPP-inspired control, the existing forecast module and that module plus the trigger. This is our follow-up experiment, not an existing result. Approximate geometry, limited layouts and non-responsive or scripted pedestrians constrain interpretation; a controller’s rejection of motion does not prove a passage physically impassable.

6. **Proposal revisions.** The five-page main document connects shared urban space, street furniture and pedestrian encounters to recorded variables, local spatial units, matched comparisons and public-space implications. It defines abbreviations, separates methods from findings, explains negative results and distinguishes completed work from hypotheses. Detailed software and engineering settings remain in optional reproduction notes. Headings are black, and figures, tables and seven references remain within the five-page main limit.

7. **AI record and preservation.** The expanded appendix includes your complete question, this complete response and three original screenshots concerning implementation, comparison choices and review requests. Its short disclosure focuses on code assistance, experimental checks and document revision; it omits the earlier topic-selection discussion. Historical screenshots are identified as such. Previous proposals, frozen code and experimental records are retained. No new training or simulation was needed.
